citations.locator: abstract page (first sentence names spin-polarized 7Li atoms)

Li.summary: Evidence of Bose-Einstein condensation in spin-polarised 7Li atoms, from the 1995 APS abstract. The page reports evidence for condensation, not a direct atom-number measurement.

citations.title: Bose-Einstein Condensation of Chromium
citations.locator: abstract page; isotope 52Cr named in the abstract

Cr.summary: Bose-Einstein condensation of chromium, with the isotope 52Cr named in the 2005 APS abstract.

Sr.summary: Two strontium isotopes have Bose-Einstein condensates: 84Sr (first realised 2009) and 88Sr (first realised 2010, by sympathetic cooling with 87Sr).

citations.title: Bose-Einstein Condensation of Strontium
citations.locator: abstract page, first sentence: 'We report on the attainment of Bose-Einstein condensation with ultracold strontium atoms.'; isotope identified as 84Sr
citations.quote: We report on the attainment of Bose-Einstein condensation with ultracold strontium atoms.

citations.title: Bose-Einstein condensation of 88Sr through sympathetic cooling with 87Sr
citations.locator: abstract page, first sentence: 'We report Bose-Einstein condensation of Sr88, which has a small, negative s-wave scattering length (a88=-2a0).'
citations.quote: We report Bose-Einstein condensation of Sr88, which has a small, negative s-wave scattering length (a88=-2a0).

citations.title: Strongly Dipolar Bose-Einstein Condensate of Dysprosium
citations.locator: abstract page, first sentence: 'We report the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of the most magnetic element, dysprosium.'; 164Dy named on the page
citations.quote: We report the Bose-Einstein condensation (BEC) of the most magnetic element, dysprosium.

Dy.summary: Bose-Einstein condensation of dysprosium, the most magnetic element, with the condensed isotope 164Dy named in the 2011 APS abstract.

Er.summary: Bose-Einstein condensation of erbium-168, reported in the 2012 APS abstract as pure condensates of up to 7 x 10^4 atoms.

H.summary: Hydrogen is a main constituent of stars. NASA states that the first generation of stars (Population III) were made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium, and describes the Sun as a ball of hydrogen and helium. This is a statement about stars that NASA describes, not a claim about every star.

citations.title: First Stars: Composition - NASA Science
citations.locator: Main text: first generation of stars made almost entirely of hydrogen and helium (page read via WebFetch)

Ne.summary: Neon is used in gas-discharge tubes (neon signs). When electrically energised, neon gas gives an orange-red light, and the gases emit light at characteristic wavelengths when electrically energised. Plasma display use is not sourced here.

citations.title: Luminous Script Signs: The Origins of the 'Neon Sign' - NIST
citations.locator: Colour statements for neon, and the statement that gases release a specific characteristic wavelength of photons (page read via WebFetch)

Ar.summary: Argon is used in gas-discharge tubes (neon-type signs). When electrically energised, argon gas gives a blue light, per NIST. Plasma display and lamp fill use are not sourced here.

citations.title: Luminous Script Signs: The Origins of the 'Neon Sign' - NIST
citations.locator: Colour statement for argon ('This gas produces a blue color.') and the characteristic-wavelength statement (page read via WebFetch)
citations.quote: This gas produces a blue color.

N.summary: Nitrogen gas in the upper atmosphere produces auroras. Energetic particles collide with oxygen and nitrogen atoms at about 100 to 400 km altitude and emit light; nitrogen contributes blue and purple. NOAA's National Calibration Center describes this.

citations.title: NOAA National Calibration Center - Aurora
citations.locator: Aurora mechanism and colour list (Oxygen: green and red, Nitrogen: blue and purple) (page read via WebFetch)

O.summary: Oxygen gas in the upper atmosphere produces auroras. Energetic particles excite oxygen, which gives off green and red light; NASA states that oxygen excited to different energy levels can produce green and red.

citations.title: Auroras - NASA Science
citations.locator: Which gases emit light: 'Oxygen excited to different energy levels can produce green and red.' (page read via WebFetch)
citations.quote: Oxygen excited to different energy levels can produce green and red.
